entities.name: Gaius Sallustius Crispus Passienus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Gaius Sallustius Passienus Crispus was a prominent figure in the Roman Empire during the first century.

He held the consulship twice, and was stepfather of the future emperor Nero.

Born around 20 CE, Crispus's early life remains shrouded in mystery.

As a seasoned military leader, he played a crucial role in the Roman campaigns against Germania during the reign of Emperor Claudius.

Crispus's tenure as consul (34-33 BCE and 22-21 BCE) was marked by notable achievements, including the construction of roads and public buildings across Rome.

The Roman Senate eventually stripped Crispus of his consulship in favor of his son-in-law, Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, after discovering an alleged affair with a Vestal Virgin.

Crispus's legacy extends to his impact on the early imperial Rome, particularly through his influence on the reign of Nero.

One notable anecdote tells of Crispus being instrumental in securing the Senate's approval for Nero's rise to power.

The passage of time has left little clear evidence of Crispus's personal life, but it is well-documented that he died at 47 CE.

the most celebrated conversationalists of the Julio-Claudian court. He served as consul twice (consul ordinarius in 27 CE and suffect consul in 44 CE), governed Asia as proconsul, and was notably twice married: first to Domitia (sister of the emperor Domitian's father, Domitius Ahenobarbus), and second to Agrippina the Younger — the future mother of the Emperor Nero and one of the most powerful women in Roman imperial history. His second marriage, by which he passed his substantial fortune to Agrippina, was particularly significant: Passienus died in 47 CE (reportedly poisoned, possibly by Agrippina), and his wealth helped finance Agrippina's subsequent political rise and ultimately contributed to Nero's imperial succession.

Passienus Crispus was the adopted son of Gaius Sallustius Crispus (the historian Sallust's great-nephew, a powerful Augustan-era adviser), from whom he inherited both name and property. This anecdote captures the dangerous comedy of the Julio-Claudian court, where wit was both currency and peril.
